title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Dual-Target Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery Under Strict Homology Constraints
abstract: The worldwide escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe challenge to modern public health, necessitating novel classes of therapeutic agents. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent highly promising alternatives to small-molecule antibiotics due to their co-evolutionary resilience and rapid membrane disruption dynamics. However, translating computational AMP leads into clinical drug candidates remains bottlenecked by off-target cytotoxicity, predominantly hemolytic activity against mammalian erythrocytes. Although pretrained foundational protein language models (PLMs) have rapidly advanced molecular property prediction, current architectures frequently isolate antibacterial potency and cytotoxicity into disconnected single-task pipelines or succumb to catastrophic performance drops under strict homology-controlled evaluations. Recently, the Quantitative Mapping of Antimicrobial Peptides (QMAP) benchmark proposed that frozen PLM embeddings show weak linearly accessible features for hemolytic activity (HC50) resulting in poor rank correlation ({rho} < 0.25) on out-of-distribution sequence splits. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end multi-task parameter-efficien

title: Bayesian Neural Networks for Uncertainty‑Aware Toxicity Prediction of Metallic Nanoparticles
abstract: Nanoparticle cytotoxicity prediction remains challenging due to the complex interplay of physicochemical properties and experimental conditions, compounded by the critical need for uncertainty quantification in safety assessments. Here, we present a hybrid computational framework integrating Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR) feature engineering with Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) to predict metallic nanoparticle toxicity while explicitly quantifying predictive uncertainty. Using a curated dataset of 1,363 experimental records (25 nanoparticle formulations) from multiple in vitro studies, with every model evaluated on formulations unseen during training, we implemented a three-stage pipeline: (i) domain-guided preprocessing with multicollinearity assessment, (ii) benchmarking of deterministic classifiers (Random Forest, SVM, Multi-Layer Perceptron and three simpler models), and (iii) variational Bayesian inference for probabilistic classification. In repeated formulation-grouped cross-validation Random Forest discriminated best (ROC-AUC = 0.974), followed by logistic regression (0.967), which was better calibrated on held-out formulations (ECE 0.046 versus 0.130).
venue: Toxicological sciences : an official journal of the Society of Toxicology

title: RadMultiBench: A Reproducible Dual-Task Benchmark Exposing the Limits of Pre-Trained Vision-Language Models Across Thoracic and Breast Imaging
abstract: We present RadMultiBench, a multimodal benchmark of 6,148 medical images paired with expert radiological impressions across five categories--Breast Cancer, Lung Benign, Lung Malignant, Pneumonia, and Tuberculosis--targeting two core clinical tasks: automated report generation and disease classification. To enable reliable, repeatable experimentation, we provide a reproducible pipeline for data ingestion, de-identification, split management, and standardized reporting of text and classification metrics, facilitating dataset versioning and continuous benchmark testing. We compare three architectures: (1) a classical CNN-RNN with Bahdanau attention (ResNet-LSTM), (2) a general-domain vision-language (V-L) prefix-projection model (CLIP-GPT), and (3) a domain-specific V-L prefix-projection model (BioViL-T). Results reveal a sharp performance divide: the ResNet-LSTM attains near-perfect classification (99.5% accuracy) and is the only model to generate coherent reports (BLEU-4 = 0.021), whereas both prefix-projection models catastrophically fail generation (BLEU-4 [≤] 0.0001); moreover, the domain-specific BioViL-T also fails classification (11.5% accuracy). title: Antimicrobial Resistance: Advances in Novel Antibiotics and Combination Therapy Approaches
HGSAF: Heterogeneous graph structural alignment and distillation model with attentive fusion for microbe-drug association prediction
abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance necessitates AI-driven computational strategies to navigate the molecular diversity landscape of microbe-drug interactions. While graph neural networks have shown promise in predicting such associations, existing methods struggle with the intertwined challenges of processing topological and semantic features in isolation and handling severe class imbalance inherent in biomedical datasets. In this work, we devised a heterogeneous graph structural alignment and distillation with an attentive fusion model to predict microbe-drug associations. Our model constructs heterogeneous biological graphs alongside meta-path-induced subgraphs to capture complementary views of microbial and drug entities. A layer-adaptive graph transformer is devised to simultaneously encode topological and positional information while mitigating noise and over-smoothing. Critically, we introduce a reciprocal distillation module for dual-path heterogeneous graph learning that mutually transfers structural and semantic knowledge between pathways, eliminating the need for explicit negative sampling during representation alignment. title: Generative Models for Novel Enzymatic Reactions: How Far Do They Go?
abstract: Enzyme function prediction is a long-standing problem in biology, and deep learning methods have recently become popular to improve performance on this task. While most of these models focus on classifying enzymes or mapping them to known reactions, predicting unknown biochemical reactions remains underexplored. Here we thoroughly examine an approach that generates reactions absent from the training data from the enzyme alone. Existing methods such as BLASTp or CLIPZyme cannot, by design, output reactions that are absent from their training data or were not supplied at inference. The closest prior model, RxnPred, reports high fingerprint-similarity scores on held-out enzymes, a less stringent criterion than exact recovery, but fails to recover the correct answer on unseen reactions. We present a structure-conditioned generative model that outputs a complete reaction, reactants and products, and evaluate it on EnzymeMap_x, a reaction-disjoint benchmark in which no test reaction appears in training, under exact, stereo-respecting scoring. On this benchmark, within 400 sampled candidates, the model generates the complete, correct reaction for 25.0% of the subset of test enzyme--reacti

title: Coarse-graining genome-scale metabolic models for dynamic, multi-scale simulations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in gel environments
abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by coupled interactions between microenvironment conditions and the intracellular adaptations that emerge in response external metabolic cues. For pathogenic microbes such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these interactions can rapidly generate heterogeneous sub-populations that exhibit adaptations for sustaining host infection and resisting antibiotic treatment. Technological strides in -omics data collection, combined with robust computational tools like genome-scale metabolic models (GEM) for predicting cellular metabolism, have yielded promising multi-scale depictions of microbial population development in simulated spatial environments. These multi-scale model simulations help establish and evaluate mechanistic contexts for how infection-enhancing behaviors might emerge in the population or be influenced by variable perturbations in the biological system. However, the number and rigorous tuning of parameters influencing the connections between intracellular-extracellular events pose barriers when shaping simulations to different in vitro systems of interest. title: PartiDesign: A structure-sequence co-design paradigm for practical all-to-all biomolecules design
abstract: Engineering interactions among biomolecules offers a route to creating new biological functions. Although unified models have advanced biomolecular structure prediction and design, efficient and controllable generation across molecular modalities remains challenging. A key challenge is to couple three-dimensional structure generation with sequence or chemical-identity design across chemically diverse systems. Here, we introduce PartiDesign, a unified structure-sequence co-design model that extends the partially latent framework of La-Proteina to proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules. PartiDesign jointly generates molecular structures and their corresponding sequences or chemical identities, while providing fine-grained control over secondary structure, chemical bonding and amino acid preferences. Across diverse benchmarks for the de novo design of proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules against specified targets, PartiDesign achieved the highest estimated successful-design throughput among the evaluated methods on most benchmarks under the adopted compute-budget protocols. title: RNA-X: Modeling RNA interactions to design binder RNA and simultaneously target multiple molecules of different types
abstract: RNA interactions with proteins, other RNA molecules, and DNA play essential roles in numerous cellular processes and underpin a wide range of therapeutic mechanisms. Consequently, modeling these interactions is critical for understanding biological systems and designing novel RNA-based therapeutics. However, designing RNA sequences that selectively and strongly bind to a specific target remains a major challenge due to the vast sequence space and the current limitations of experimental and computational methods. In this study, we introduce RNA-X, the first RNA interaction foundation model which is based on masked language modeling for representation learning, conditional RNA design, and optimization. For the first time, RNA-X enables (i) RNA design targeting not only proteins but also other RNA and DNA molecules, and (ii) simultaneous design against multiple targets. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that RNA-X generates RNA sequences with natural structural characteristics and surpasses state-of-the-art methods in protein targeting. We experimentally validate RNA-X in vitro, where a RNAX-designed RNA targeting the 5'UTR of the androgen receptor (AR) mRNA was shown to reduce bo

title: Molecular insights and antimicrobial evaluation of 4-aminopyridinium-5-sulfosalicylate sesquihydrate: A dual in vitro and in silico approach
abstract: This study reports a detailed investigation of the organic salt 4-aminopyridinium-5-sulfosalicylate sesquihydrate (4A5SS) through an integrated In Vitro and In Silico approach. The present work combines antimicrobial studies, Density Functional Theory (DFT), Dynamics simulations, Docking, and ADME/Toxicity evaluation to explore its structural, electronic, optical, biological, and pharmacokinetic attributes. Determination of the lattice dimensions and overall crystalline arrangement was achieved via SC-XRD analysis, accompanied by spectroscopic profiling (FT-IR, FT-Raman, and UV-Vis) to investigate optical and vibrational behaviours. Theoretical calculations executed using DFT with the B3LYP/6-31 + G(d,p) basis set demonstrated good consistency with the experimental crystallographic geometry. Frontier molecular orbital (HOMO-LUMO) evaluations were employed to examine charge-transfer dynamics and biological reactivity, while MEP mapping delineated reactive centres relevant to intermolecular hydrogen bonding regions. Hirshfeld surface topology and 2D fingerprint plots corroborated the specific contributions of both intra- and intermolecular contact networks within the crystal matrix.

title: Programmable interphyla communication for Staphylococcus aureus by transferability of homoserine lactone sensors between Bacillales bacteria
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive opportunistic pathogen of the order Bacillales and a frequent member of human-associated microbiomes. Despite its clinical relevance, engineering S. aureus and the communities it inhabits remains limited by a shortage of well-characterized genetic tools for precise control of gene expression and intercellular signaling. Biosensors for homoserine lactones (HSLs) are widely used in Gram-negative bacteria, as HSLs are small, passively diffusible signaling molecules for and their sensors are tightly regulated. Here, we show that synthetically designed HSL sensors using LuxR-family regulators are highly functional in S. aureus. Notably, synthetic designs previously built for the Gram-positive model Bacillus subtilis, a distantly related Bacillales, transferred functionally and establish repurposing the genetic toolbox as an effective strategy for importing these functions into S. aureus. Sensor performance correlated strongly between the two Bacillales, and activation in S. aureus reached 55-fold, exceeding the dynamic range of reported inducible systems. We further demonstrate tightly regulated, programmable interphyla communication between Gram

title: GeneEmbedLLM: Harnessing Large Language Models for Gene Functional Embedding and Association Prediction
abstract: Effective and high-quality gene function representations are crucial for bioinformatics tasks. While biological knowledge about genes is inherently textual, encompassing functional descriptions and pathway annotations, current methods often rely on single-source, non-textual data, failing to capture the rich semantic information in multi-source gene annotations. In this paper, we propose GeneEmbedLLM, a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered framework for generating universal, semantically-aware gene embeddings. The proposed approach advances the gene representation learning through multi-source structured text integration from five authoritative databases and attribute-aware attention based on Longformer architecture and contrastive learning. Experimental results on diverse downstream tasks, ranging from molecular interactions and phenotypic dependencies to epigenetic regulation, confirm the validity and effectiveness of our proposed approach, where competitive performance is achieved across all evaluated benchmarks. We further validate the quality of the generated embeddings through comprehensive analyses, including embedding visualizations, intra-pathway similarity assessments, abla

title: Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

title: Technologies in Natural Product Research: From High-Resolution Separation and Structural Elucidation to Dereplication, Metabolomics and Drug Discovery
RPFace: From biased structural benchmarks to generalizable RNA-protein interface prediction
abstract: Modeling protein-RNA complexes with co-folding and docking methods is routine, yet these methods are evaluated on benchmarks whose composition mirrors the deposited structures on which they were trained or tuned, leaving open whether their reported performance reflects true generalization. Here, we focus the evaluation on the region that carries the biological signal: the binding interface. For the first time, we construct and release a fair benchmark that stratifies protein-RNA data into distinct structural and experimental groups, providing a more stringent test of generalization than aggregate averages. On this benchmark, we find that accuracy of detecting the binding site using co-folding methods is concentrated in ribosomal complexes and varies systematically with factors such as experimental modality. For docking methods, it is reliable only when the input conformations are already close to the bound state, and it is inconsistent across RNA classes. Both families of methods fail to transfer to in vivo CLIP experiments. title: Classifying tumors from broad category to hierarchical molecular subtype: an interpretable hierarchical framework for precision oncology
abstract: Precise tumor subtype classification is important for guiding personalized treatment, characterizing tumor heterogeneity, and investigating molecular mechanisms. However, most existing multi-label classification models use flat architectures and do not fully exploit the inherent hierarchical relationships and biological constraints among tumor types, which limits their performance and interpretability in complex, fine-grained pan-cancer classification. Here, we present the cancer Hallmark-based Hierarchical Recursive Model (HHRM) for pan-cancer hierarchical multi-label classification. HHRM integrates hierarchical label structures with recursive neural networks, enabling simultaneous modeling of multi-level dependencies from broad cancer categories to specific subtypes. We trained the model on a comprehensive pan-cancer cohort of 11,476 samples spanning 26 primary cancer types and 405 subtypes across up to eight hierarchical levels. HHRM achieved an accuracy of 0.7924 for predicting hierarchical tumor subtypes and was further evaluated on a validation dataset of 887 samples. Compared with other hierarchical modeling frameworks, HHRM achieved higher accuracy in all three output modes

title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence rep-resentations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association netwo

V-SWITCH: A single-vector OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter of live RNA virus infections
abstract: Fluorescent reporters of viral infection are powerful tools for studying viral pathogenesis and host-pathogen interactions. Here, we present V-SWITCH, a highly modular, single-vector, cell-based OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter that enables robust detection of viral infection in living cells. V-SWITCH is based on a split mNeonGreen (mNG) system employing a release-and-capture mechanism. In the "OFF" state, the mNG3A(1-10) fragment is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum via a Sec61 transmembrane domain, while the mNG(11) fragment, fused to BFP, is constitutively expressed in the nucleus. Upon infection, the viral protease cleaves a protease cleavage site (PCS) adjacent to the mNG3A(1-10) fragment, liberating it for translocation into the nucleus. There, it complements mNG(11) to reconstitute fluorescence. The constitutive BFP serves as both an expression control and a nuclear segmentation marker for image analysis. Each module in this dual-cassette design is flanked by unique restriction sites allowing rapid swapping of virus-specific PCS, split fluorophores, membrane anchors, and promoters. title: AI-Guided Structure-Aware Modeling and Thermal Proteomics Reveal Direct Demethylzeylasteral-ACLY Interaction
abstract: Identifying the direct molecular targets of bioactive natural products remains a central challenge in chemical biology. Here we present an integrated experimental-computational framework, that combines matrix-augmented thermal proteomics with HoloGNN, a holistic graph neural network, to systematically prioritize and validate protein-ligand interactions. Benchmarking with PDBbind datasets HoloGNN achieves state-of-the-art performance. Applying this framework to 50 structurally diverse natural products identified Demethylzeylasteral as a direct interactor of ACLY. Orthogonal biochemical assays confirmed micromolar binding and enzymatic inhibition. In an imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like mouse model, Demethylzeylasteral reduced disease severity and inflammatory cytokine expression. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed that Demethylzeylasteral reverses keratinocyte hyperproliferation and suppresses ACLY-dependent lipid metabolic reprogramming. Together, this scalable, closed-loop strategy integrates thermal proteomics and machine learning to uncover direct targets of natural products and provides mechanistic evidence linking ACLY inhibition to therapeutic modulation of inflammatory path

title: PhenoMe: An interactive AI framework for interpretable, microscopy-driven phenotyping
abstract: Extracting meaningful biological patterns from microscopy image datasets requires tools that quantitatively connect visual similarities and experimental context. Deep learning models, and in particular novel foundation models, have the capacity to translate images into high-dimensional embeddings that can better represent complex visual patterns. Using these complex representations analytically and linking them to experimental information, it is possible to build advanced exploratory and phenotyping capabilities. Here, we present PhenoMe, an open-source, model-agnostic framework to handle pretrained foundation model-derived image representations alongside quantitative image properties and experimental metadata. PhenoMe integrates multiple scriptable and interactive workflows for embedding space visualisation, dimensionality reduction and clustering, similarity-based comparison and retrieval of representative images for each phenotype, among others. It also supports correlation analyses that link the embedding structure to interpretable image properties. title: The Digital Twin Paradigm in Head and Neck Cancer: Clinical Opportunities and Challenges
abstract:
Unlabelled

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) represents a significant public health challenge. Its treatment is characterized by high anatomical complexity and a critical need for functional preservation of speech, swallowing, and respiration. While multimodality care, including surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, has substantially improved patient survival, there are still high rates of life-altering toxicities and low response rates to immunotherapy. Current clinical decision-making largely relies on "digital snapshots"-static representations derived from population-based statistics and time point-specific imaging-which usually fail to account for the rapid anatomical and biological change during the course of treatment. Digital twins hold great promise in accelerating scientific breakthroughs and transforming oncology treatment and precision medicine through the creation of high-fidelity virtual patient representations that integrate real-time biological, anatomical, and clinical data. Profile of Genes Encoding Antimicrobial Resistance and Virulence in 3963 Escherichia coli Isolates

Artificial Intelligence in Medical Research: Emerging Concepts, Applications, and Challenges
In Vitro Activity of Cefiderocol against Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii
RNA-targeted aminopyridine compounds provide a new antifungal strategy
abstract: While RNA is an emerging therapeutic target class, progress is limited by a shortage of well-defined targets in which ligand binding is coupled to measurable function. The group I intron, a self-splicing ribozyme essential in fungal mitochondria but absent from humans, offers both a tractable platform for exploring first principles of small molecule-RNA targeting and a selective antifungal target. We recalibrated an intron-splicing assay to approximate cellular conditions and performed an extensive, cryo-EM-guided structure-activity relationship campaign against the Candida albicans mtLSU intron. Ligands containing a flexible diamine outperformed conformationally constrained analogues, suggesting a general principle for engaging dynamic RNA surfaces and yielding lead aminopyridine 56 (IC 21.6 nM). Compound 56 synergizes with amphotericin B against C. albicans, suggesting a path for combination therapies. RT-qPCR confirmed direct target engagement in cells. This work establishes the fungal group I intron as a viable, mechanistically distinct antifungal target and a model platform for RNA-targeted discovery.

title: scCont: Interpretable Contrastive Learning for Functional Characterization of Cellular State Transitions
abstract: Timecourse single-cell RNA (scRNA) datasets have become indispensable biological tools for studying and uncovering the underlying regulatory processes driving continuous cell-state transitions such as the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. However, these highly fluid, non-linear gene program dynamics remain difficult to disentangle. While deep neural network models can effectively map complex topologies, they are biological black boxes, lacking the gene-level interpretability required by experimental practitioners. Here, we introduce scCont, a fully unsupervised contrastive learning framework for extracting interpretable functional transition units from scRNA-seq data. Rather than relying on explicit temporal labels or clustering priors, scCont uses an unsupervised k-nearest neighbors approach to project local transcriptomic neighborhoods into a low-dimensional embedding. During post-training analysis, scCont employs Shapley network attribution to determine gene-latent relationships, mapping latent dimensions directly into functional gene programs. We quantitatively and qualitatively validate this representation by demonstrating that scCont captures biologically interpretable dy

title: Towards a foundation model for raw nanopore signal through discrete tokenization
abstract: Nanopore sequencing reads nucleic acids as changes in ionic current that carry information beyond the base sequence. Self-supervised pretrained models have advanced genomic sequence modeling and single-cell analysis, but remain underexplored for raw nanopore signals, which are continuous and lack a native token vocabulary. Here we present Brieno, an approach combining reconstruction-based tokenization through residual vector quantization with a Transformer for contextual representation learning. We pretrain the Transformer using masked-token prediction on raw nanopore signals from 118 million reads. With frozen or fine-tuned features, the model identifies species without requiring reference genomes. It complements Dorado by accurately classifying reads left unclassified in native-barcode demultiplexing, approaches Dorado's basecalling performance across six genomes, and exceeds Dorado's specialized 5-methylcytosine model as well as a dedicated 6-methyladenine caller. Brieno also supports accurate CpG methylation detection with limited labeled data. title: Anticancer activity of sodium propionate in hepatocellular carcinoma cells via downregulation of HDAC2 and HDAC6
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is an aggressive malignancy driven by epigenetic dysregulation. This study investigates the anticancer potential of sodium propionate (SP) as an epigenetic modulator targeting histone deacetylases (HDACs) using an integrated in silico and in vitro approach. Bioinformatics analyses were conducted using publicly available HCC transcriptomic datasets from GEO database, disease gene database (GeneCards database), and chemical-gene interaction networks (Comparative Toxicogenomic Database) to identify potential therapeutic targets, HDAC2 and HDAC6 as key therapeutic targets in HCC. Computational ADMET screening indicated SP possesses favourable drug-likeness, high oral bioavailability, and low toxicity. Molecular docking and 500-ns molecular dynamics simulations showed stable SP binding to HDAC2, with ligand RMSD of 1.5-2.0 Å, protein RMSD of 3.0-4.5 Å, and active-site RMSF < 1.0 Å, supported by persistent Zn²⁺ coordination and hydrophobic interactions. In vitro evaluations in HepG2 cells revealed distinct dose-dependent cytotoxicity (IC₅₀ = 8.2 mM) and pronounced morphological alterations. title: MitoDecode: quantitative phenotypic decoding of mitochondrial stress states from fluorescence images
abstract: The quantitative measurement of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence images of cells remains a challenging task. Existing methods rely on mitochondrial segmentation, manually predefined features, and discrete phenotype severity classes, which are prone to error and bias. Here, we present MitoDecode, a deep learning network that automatically assesses type and severity of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence microscopy images. MitoDecode eliminates the need for mitochondrial segmentation, is parameter-free, and operates across both diffraction-limited and super-resolution optical imaging modalities. It assigns a phenotypic probability profile for each individual cell, indicating both type and severity of phenotypic stress. The readout thus enables comparisons between different stressors and provides clues for underlying mechanisms. Furthermore, the method captures phenotypic shifts continuously across treatment doses, revealing subtle variations that would otherwise be missed. We demonstrate MitoDecode's adaptability across diverse cell types, imaging modalities, and stress conditions, and show that it can reliably detect mitochondrial phenotypes, even when stressors target non-

title: Phage lysates are reservoirs of biologically active quorum sensing signals
abstract: Bacteriophage lysates are widely used to study phage-bacterial interactions and are typically applied after filtration without further purification. As a result, host-derived metabolites produced during phage propagation are transferred alongside phage particles, yet the biological consequences of this carryover remain largely unexplored. Here, we show that the Pseudomonas aeruginosa quorum sensing signal PQS persists in a bioactive state in phage lysates for at least one year. In contrast, the quorum sensing molecules 3OC12-HSL and C4-HSL are rapidly degraded. We demonstrate that PQS stability is caused by its association with outer membrane vesicles, which protect the signal from degradation. PQS from phage lysates induces production of the virulence factor pyocyanin and increases mortality in a Galleria mellonella model of P. aeruginosa infection. Importantly, PQS carryover does not explain previous reports of phage mediated activation of the PQS system, as this response also occurs in PQS free phage lysates, establishing phage lysate-mediated signal transfer and phage-induced signaling as distinct mechanisms. title: Multi-objective domain adaptation for pan-cancer transfer of pharmacogenomic drug response to patient tumours
abstract: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. title: Structural modeling and <i>in silico</i> screening of antimicrobial peptides targeting BauE in <i>Acinetobacter baumannii</i>
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that relies on ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters for siderophore-mediated iron acquisition. BauE, the ATP-binding subunit of the ferric acinetobactin transporter, drives ATP hydrolysis to power iron import and therefore represents a potential therapeutic target. In this study, an integrated computational approach was employed to characterize the structure of BauE and identify antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) predicted to interact with functionally important regions. Since no experimental structure of BauE is currently available, three-dimensional models were generated using AlphaFold, Robetta, and trRosetta and refined through structural validation and 500 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The AlphaFold-predicted model exhibited the highest structural stability and was selected for further analyses. Binding pocket prediction revealed a druggable cavity located near the Q-loop and Walker B motif, regions essential for ATP hydrolysis. title: In silico identification of drug compounds to arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase of Proteus mirabilis to combat its antibiotic resistance using an integrated bioinformatics: subtractive proteomics, molecular docking, MD simulation and DFT studies
abstract: Proteus mirabilis is a major opportunistic Gram-negative pathogen causing complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs), particularly in catheterized patients. Although several antibiotics, including streptomycin, erythromycin, and sparfloxacin, remain effective against some infections, the growing spread of multidrug-resistant P. mirabilis strains has created an urgent need to identify new therapeutic targets and treatment options. Using a subtractive proteomics approach, this study identified potential therapeutic targets in P. mirabilis. Among the 417 essential pathogen-specific proteins, 11 were identified as druggable, virulence-associated, and antibiotic resistance-related proteins, making them promising novel therapeutic targets against P. mirabilis. Among them, nine are enzymatic proteins involved in crucial biological pathways such as glycan and amino acid biosynthesis, energy metabolism, cellular signaling, and genetic information processing. title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable SI Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generating novel AMPs with desired properties using generative SI (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable SI (XSI) methods to validate the GenSI model and derive biological insights. In this work, we fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. To advance the interpretability and reliability of the generative model, we applied Explainable SI (XSI) techniques. Specifically, we used a probing classifier and a regressor to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we validated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. Overall, these methods provide mechanistic insight into the model's decision-making process, offering a principled basis for trusting the sequences

title: Virtual screening and molecular docking of flavonoid compounds as BACE-1 inhibitors for Alzheimer's Disease: identification of Betagarin as a promising nutraceutical lead candidate
abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder accounting for 60-70% of dementia cases globally, with the β-site amyloid precursor protein cleaving enzyme-1 (BACE-1) representing one of the most intensively studied therapeutic targets due to its rate-limiting role in amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide production. Despite decades of drug discovery efforts, no approved BACE-1 inhibitor has successfully demonstrated both efficacy and safety in large-scale clinical trials, largely owing to off-target toxicity and poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. This study presents a multi-tiered structure-based virtual screening of 1,870 flavonoid compounds against the catalytic domain of BACE-1 (PDB ID: 2ZJN) using AutoDock Vina. Ligand preparation was performed with Open Babel v3.1.1, and docking was executed within a 30 × 30 × 30 Å grid box centred on the catalytic aspartyl dyad (Asp32 and Asp228). Drug-likeness was evaluated using Lipinski's Rule of Five, and in silico toxicity was assessed via the OSIRIS Property Explorer across four risk categories. Betagarin, a natural flavonoid constituent of Beta vulgaris (beetroot), was selected as the primary lead candida

title: Delineating the structural distortions in hIAPP protofibrils by rationally designed hexapeptides using computer simulations
abstract: Disease-associated fibrillation of human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP), also referred to as human amylin, plays a pivotal role in the etiology of type 2 diabetes (T2D). The hIAPP fibrillation leads to the generation of cytotoxic β-sheet-rich oligomers and protofibrils that contribute to the apoptosis of pancreatic β-cells. Potter et al. reported hIAPP fragment peptide ANFLVH (residues 13-18, designated as AF6) as a potent inhibitor of hIAPP fibrillation. Notably, AF6 blocked IAPP fibrillation in vitro and in human islet cell cultures, which noticeably enhanced the viability of islet cells. In this work, a structure-based virtual screening approach was employed to screen a library of hexapeptides generated through systematic mutations in AF6, and the potential of the top hit peptides for the conformational destabilization of full-length ζ-shaped hIAPP protofibrils (PDB: 7YKW) has been assessed using molecular docking, MM-PBSA, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. title: The IFN-γ-inducible GTPase IIGP1 regulates mitochondrial remodeling and immunometabolic reprogramming during inflammatory macrophage polarization
abstract: Macrophages are key effector cells of the innate immune system that undergo dynamic polarization into functionally distinct phenotypic states, ranging from classically activated inflammatory (M1) to alternatively activated (M2) macrophages. Inflammatory macrophage polarization requires coordinated integration of cytokine signaling, metabolic reprogramming, and mitochondrial remodeling. However, the molecular effectors that control inflammatory signaling for mitochondrial metabolism and remodeling remain poorly defined. Using quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics, we identified Interferon-inducible GTPase 1 (IIGP1) as one of the most robustly induced proteins during inflammatory macrophage polarization. Its expression is governed by the IFN-{gamma}-JAK-STAT1 signaling axis and is crucial for this polarization process. IIGP1-deficient macrophages exhibited significantly impaired iNOS induction, nitric oxide production, pro-inflammatory gene expression, co-stimulatory surface marker expression, and morphological remodeling. Further, IIGP1 associates with mitochondria and its absence impairs key characteristics of inflammatory macrophages, including glycolytic metabolic repro

title: Discovery of P1-P2 depeptidized boronic acid based Plasmodium falciparum SUB1 inhibitor
abstract: The Plasmodium falciparum subtilisin-like serine protease 1 (PfSUB1) is an essential enzyme required for parasite egress from host red blood cells and represents a promising target for antimalarial drugs. Peptidic boronic acids are potent reported PfSUB1 inhibitors, however their drug-likeness is limited by their pronounced peptidic character. Based on molecular docking studies using peptidic boronic acids, we designed a series of partially depeptidized PfSUB1 inhibitors by replacing the P1-P2 dipeptide fragment with a 3-aminomethylphenylboronic acid core. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) investigations targeting interaction with active-site residue Lys138 revealed that introducing a meta-carboxylate group (compound 3a) markedly enhanced inhibitory activity, yielding a low-nanomolar PfSUB1 inhibitor (IC50= 10.2 nM). Bioisosteric replacement of the carboxylic acid demonstrated that an N-acylsulfonamide group (compound 4k) retained high enzymatic potency (IC50= 13.5 nM)). title: GSET: Gene Signals from Embedding Trajectories select compact contexts for mechanistic GRN inference
abstract: Mechanistic inference of gene regulatory networks from temporal transcriptomic data can become computationally prohibitive at transcriptome scale, making gene selection an important determinant of which regulatory relationships can be recovered. However, gene selection for GRN inference commonly relies on static expression or co-expression structure, rather than prioritizing dynamically informative genes whose temporal patterns capture how transcriptional programs change and relate to one another. We introduce GSET (Gene Signals from Embedding Trajectories), an upstream retrieval framework that extracts dynamic information from temporal gene embeddings using two complementary signals: an optimal transport residual, which captures gene-specific deviations from global embedding movement, and a KL divergence, which detects changes in local co-expression neighborhoods. Temporal gene-embedding similarity identifies static transcriptional programs, whereas vectorial GSET signals represent coordinated temporal changes among genes, complementing this static structure. title: HYphlow: bringing end-to-end flow to HyPhy selection analyses, from taxon reconciliation to trait-based foreground assignment
abstract: Phylogenetic analyses of molecular evolution often require repeated manual preparation to reconcile taxa, annotate trees, execute models, and summarize results. These steps become increasingly time-consuming and difficult to standardize as the number of taxa, genes, and analytical hypotheses increases. We present HYphlow, an open-source graphical workflow developed in Python that integrates data preparation, trait-based foreground branch assignment, HyPhy execution, and structured result extraction within a single interface. HYphlow reconciles taxon labels across alignments, trees, and trait data; reconstructs ancestral states using parsimony and maximum likelihood; generates alternative foreground annotations; executes HyPhy analyses locally or through portable scripts for high-performance computing; and records analytical decisions and settings throughout the workflow. We evaluated HYphlow using simulations and two published datasets comprising cryptochrome analyses in pigeons and doves and visual opsin analyses in skinks. A name-similarity threshold of 80 reliably recovered simulated spelling variants, while consensus foreground assignment increased precision relative to parsimo

title: New perspectives in assessing environmental risks for birds: a simple TKTD framework to link growth and reproduction energy budget to chemical stress
abstract: Assessing the risk of pesticides to birds requires models that can extrapolate laboratory data to realistic exposure scenarios. In this work, we propose a new modeling framework BIRDkiss (Bird - Impact on Reproduction via Diet, keep it simple and suitable). This framework integrates a simplified Dynamic Energy Budget (DEBkiss) of organisms and the toxicokinetic-toxicodynamic (TKTD) of chemical substances according to a trait-based approach, thereby reducing the number of parameters to identify and strengthening the statistical robustness of the critical endpoints. The BIRDkiss model describes how food intake and toxicant exposure affect growth and egg production in birds over time. The model is fully embedded within an R package, including routines for calibration, validation and prediction under single-compound scenarios performed via Bayesian inference using standard data from the OECD avian reproduction tests. The BIRDkiss model also allows the simulations of scenarios under both varying food availability and multi-compound exposures based on the two classical mixture-toxicity paradigms: Concentration Addition (CA) and Independent Action (IA). abstract:
Background:

/Objectives: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a great threat to human health, and combination therapy is effective for its control. Previous work has performed for the antimicrobial quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models and synergistic antibacterial effects with clinical antibiotics of plant flavonoids. This study investigated whether antimicrobial QSAR models can be constructed for natural quinones and whether these compounds also exert extensive synergism when combined with clinical antibiotics.

Methods:

The antibacterial activities of 18 designed quinones and 11 clinical antibiotics with various antimicrobial mechanisms were determined using microbroth dilution method. Subsequently, the correlation and regression analyses between the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and physicochemical parameter of quinones were performed for the establishment of antimicrobial QSAR models. Simultaneously, induction and deduction were applied to summarize the SARs based on the antimicrobial activity changes induced by structural variations. title: Cross-Level Graph Fusion With Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Accurate Drug Repositioning
abstract: Drug repositioning accelerates the identification of novel therapeutic indications for approved compounds by leveraging established safety and pharmacokinetic profiles, thereby substantially reducing development costs and timelines. Heterogeneous graph neural networks have shown strong potential for modeling multi-relational biomedical associations among drugs, diseases, and protein targets. However, their considerable computational complexity limits scalability in high- throughput screening scenarios. Here, we present GraphKD-DR, a cross-level graph fusion framework that reconciles representational expressiveness with computational efficiency through knowledge distillation. Specifically, the teacher model integrates homogeneous similarity graphs with multi-view heterogeneous biomedical representations via Transformer-based cross-level fusion. Predictive, feature-level, and relational knowledge is then transferred from the teacher to a lightweight student model, substantially reducing model complexity while preserving predictive performance. GraphKD-DR achieves approximately 98% fewer parameters and reduces training time by 98.73-99.33%, while retaining comparable predictive perfor

title: Rigorous nested cross-validation and external generalization-gap analysis of a machine-learning classifier for U-251 glioblastoma cytotoxicity
abstract: Glioblastoma remains difficult to treat, and drug-repositioning strategies require efficient methods to evaluate chemical libraries. Here, we developed a machine-learning binary classifier for compound activity against U-251 glioblastoma cells using a corrected single-center dataset of 236 compounds evaluated under a standardized cell-viability assay. Compounds were labeled as active or inactive using a predefined viability criterion (<50% vs. ≥ 50%) within a single-point screening framework using 10 µM as the upper screening concentration. To reduce optimistic bias and information leakage, we used repeated nested cross-validation in which preprocessing, feature selection, and hyperparameter optimization were performed within the training folds. ExtraTrees was selected based on Matthews correlation coefficient, showing moderate internal performance (ROC-AUC, 0.76; balanced accuracy, 0.66; MCC, 0.36). Structural analyses using nearest-neighbor Tanimoto similarity and Bemis-Murcko scaffolds indicated that the training set was scaffold-diverse with limited series bias. However, when the locked model was applied to an independent external set of 53 compounds, all compounds were classif

title: Multi-scale computational analysis of MMP9 and SIRT1 regulatory networks and their interaction with curcumin and resveratrol in lung adenocarcinoma
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a major cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality, highlighting the need for therapeutic strategies capable of targeting multiple oncogenic pathways. In this study, an integrative computational framework that combines pharmacokinetic profiling, protein interaction network analysis, molecular docking, 200 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, MM-GBSA binding free-energy estimation, transcriptomic analysis, genomic alteration assessment, and consensus miRNA modeling was used to explore curcumin and resveratrol as potential modulators of the molecular processes associated with MMP9 and SIRT1 in LUAD. Both compounds exhibited favorable drug-likeness characteristics, gastrointestinal absorption, and predicted low acute toxicity. Network analysis identified MMP9- and SIRT1-centered interaction networks with TP53 emerging as a common central node. Molecular docking predicted favorable interactions of curcumin with MMP9 and resveratrol with SIRT1. However, SIRT1 docking validation produced an RMSD of 2.26 Å, slightly exceeding the predefined 2.0 Å threshold; therefore, the resveratrol-SIRT1 docking result was considered supportive rather than fully val

title: Design, synthesis, and evaluation of novel hydrazide and hydroxamate derivatives as potent antileukemic agents with preferential HDAC-2 inhibitory activity over class I isoform
abstract: The development of isoform-selective histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors remains a promising frontier for targeted cancer therapy, offering a strategic opportunity to maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing the adverse side effects of pan-HDAC inhibition. In this study, we present a novel series of 4-iodo-3-nitrophenyl-capped hydrazide and hydroxamate compounds that were developed, and investigated for potential to function as effective and preferential HDAC-2 inhibitors. In vitro enzyme assays revealed that this new scaffold prefers the HDAC-2 isoform over HDAC-1, which differs significantly from the non-selective reference medication, Vorinostat (SAHA). Upon testing these compounds with the propidium iodide (PI) fluorescence assay across many human cancer cell lines, we observed a remarkable, tissue-specific sensitivity. The foremost derivatives (7a, 7c, and 7d) exhibited much greater efficacy in inhibiting the growth of B-cell acute lymphoblastic (SEM) cells, exhibiting IC50 values ranging from 3.18 to 4.17 µM, surpassing the reference drug Vorinostat, which presented an IC50 of 5.23 µM. title: Linalool as a multi-targeted natural anticancer agent: review on molecular mechanisms, potency, limitations and prospects of translation
abstract: Linalool is a naturally occurring volatile monoterpene that exhibits significant anticancer potency across several malignancies via multitargeted molecular mechanisms. However, the translational research requires a clear anticancer potency with molecular targets and bioavailability data with respect to cancer type as identified via adequate cell and animal models, which lead to clinical trials. Nevertheless, the translation of linalool for clinical use is restricted by the lack of clinical trials and its limited in vivo bioavailability as reported in pre-clinical studies, high volatility and poor aqueous solubility. Therefore, this review examines the reported anticancer potency, probable molecular mechanisms, bioavailability research findings, and current nanoformulation of linalool for future application as an effective medicine. Inadequate in vivo validation and limited intravenous delivery data further highlight the need for advanced nanoformulation techniques and thorough translational studies. The literature for this review was methodically collected from research findings published between 2000 and 2025, capturing foundational and current breakthroughs on linalool's anticanc

title: Accelerating discovery and integration from RNA to Protein with R2T2P
abstract: Integrating transcriptomics and proteomics data remains an unmet challenge in the post-genomics era, discouraging researchers from pursuing integrative approaches to molecular biology research. Leveraging the power of translation profiling, we present RNA to Translation to Protein (R2T2P), a computational platform integrating genome-guided transcriptome assembly with identification of translation and proteins, including a tailored differential analysis framework and support for multiple reference transcriptomes. We applied R2T2P to investigate a cellular model of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD), where ectopic expression of the DUX4 retrogene in skeletal muscle triggers significant alterations in transcription and RNA metabolism. We uncovered hundreds of uncharacterized, highly overexpressed RNAs, including antisense and alternative transcripts, and quantified their contribution to translatome and proteome. Re-analysis of expression datasets from patient-derived myotubes and muscle biopsies validated this alternative transcriptome in FSHD patients, adding a reservoir of bona-fide novel molecular actors in a rare disease. Available at https://github.com/nfdata-omics/R2T

title: π-SPECFormer: A Mass Spectrometry-based Foundation Model for Decoding the Dark Proteome
abstract: In mass-spectrometry-based proteomics, a substantial proportion of acquired spectra remain unidentified, concealing a vast reservoir of biological variations commonly termed the "dark proteome", potentially obscuring sequence mutations, non-canonical peptides and post-translational modifications. Existing deep-learning methods largely rely on supervised training with peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs), limiting their ability to learn from the much larger pool of unannotated spectra. Here we introduce {pi}-SPECFormer, a mass-spectrometry foundation model pre-trained on 291 million spectra through a two-stage framework that combines self-supervised and PSMs-guided representation learning. {pi}-SPECFormer transfers effectively to de novo peptide sequencing, spectrum clustering and modification detection, consistently outperforming task-specific baselines. When applied to proteomic profiles from 103 individuals with lung adenocarcinoma, the model identified nine high-confidence mutated peptides, including six that were absent from the reference databases. {pi}-SPECFormer thus enables unbiased decoding of molecular complexity beyond the boundaries of the canonical proteome.

title: SPARK: Systematic Profiling of Antibiotic-Phage Response Kinetics
abstract: Phage therapy is, in practice, combination therapy: phage are almost always added to an ongoing antibiotic regimen, yet the combination is rarely designed to have a specific interaction pattern. Interactions can be antagonistic, additive or synergistic and cannot be inferred from either agent alone. Here we introduce SPARK, a method which quantifies phage antibiotic interaction from growth curves as the integrated deviation of observed growth from the growth expected under Bliss independence. We profiled 42 combinations spanning the ESKAPE pathogens and Escherichia coli with twelve antibiotics. We show that i) synergy and antagonism are resolvable within a single high-throughput assay, with the interaction determined by the phage antibiotic bacteria pairing; ii) 21 clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates differ among themselves as widely as the seven species do; and, iii) interactions change between a few hours and two days, several reversing direction. Overall, SPARK needs only a plate reader and the analysis is performed with a specific openly available web tool.

abstract: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. title: Molecular Characterization of T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia by an Optimal-Transport Based Multi-Omics Integration Framework
abstract: T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy characterized by complex heterogeneity across multiple molecular layers. Accurate subtyping is essential for understanding disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and guiding targeted therapeutic strategies. However, current diagnostic approaches are labor-intensive and time-consuming, and existing computational methods are limited by reliance on single-modality data or simple integration strategies. Effective integration of heterogeneous multi-omics data remains a major computational challenge. We present OTTER (Optimal Transport-based Transcriptomics and gEnomics Representation), a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that jointly models transcriptomic and genomic data for T-ALL molecular characterization. OTTER encodes each omics modality through a modality-specific encoder and aligns the resulting latent representations using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT), which preserves the internal geometric structure of each modality without requiring a shared feature space. title: Learning Strand-Equivariant Tokenizations of DNA with MirrorDNA
abstract: DNA has two strands, and for most regulatory label prediction tasks a sequence and its reverse complement should get same answer. Yet DNA language models are tokenized, trained and tested on one strand at a time. We show that this makes them inconsistent. BPE and $k$-mer tokenizers split 92--100\% of transcription-factor motifs differently on the two strands, and NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA change 25-31\% of their predictions when the test sequences are reverse-complemented. We introduce {\model}, a compact DNA language model with a learned tokenizer that guarantees mirror-symmetric token boundaries across reverse-complement sequences, regardless of its learned parameters. We prove that this symmetry holds through the whole model. As a result, the same model can give identical answers on both strands when the label does not depend on the strand, and can still tell the strands apart when it does, which no strand-blind model can learn. Counting only predictions that are correct on both strands, \model\ more than doubles the MCC of NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA. With 2.3M parameters, it is more accurate than the Caduceus models trained on the same data, and not significantly differe

title: DisCell: Separating Spillover from Niche Response in Spatial Transcriptomics
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics at single-cell resolution measures every cell in its place in the tissue, but diffusion and segmentation errors also add transcripts of neighboring cells to a cell's counts. This spillover makes a cell resemble its neighbors, and a response to the niche makes cells in the same niche resemble each other. Both tie a cell's expression to its surroundings. The count data alone cannot tell the two apart. Findings from single-cell transcriptomes, such as a gene program that is higher in one niche than in another or signaling genes that change depending on the neighborhood, may therefore be artifacts of spillover. Current models describe a cell by its intrinsic state together with either its niche response or spillover, but none models all three. We present DisCell, the first method that models all three components jointly and measures how robust each finding is to spillover. DisCell is a generative model that describes single-cell gene expression profiles in terms of two latent variables, an intrinsic state and a response to the niche, and adds spillover from its neighbors as a separate term. DisCell fits the model at increasing levels of spillover and recomputes

title: Predicting Transcriptional Responses to Unseen Compounds through Context Modeling and Multi-View Transfer
abstract: Predicting drug-induced transcriptional responses could support in silico screening of new compounds, yet existing models barely use the compound: on a drug-blind L1000 benchmark, removing the drug input from seven published models changes accuracy by at most 0.012 Pearson correlation. They capture shared cellular and experimental variation while overlooking the compound-specific signals that distinguish drug effects. We present UnDetect, a framework that separates contextual variation from compound effects to predict responses to transcriptionally unprofiled compounds. UnDetect integrates chemical structure, annotated targets, mechanisms of action and Cell Painting morphology into a normalized multi-view kernel that accommodates incomplete compound information, and transfers residual responses within and across profiled cell lines, so that pharmacological and phenotypic relationships inform predictions beyond chemical similarity. On a drug-blind benchmark, where the paired control reveals the assay plate, UnDetect is the only model to beat a network that ignores the compound, in every fold; on a within-plate score that is zero for any compound-blind prediction, it reaches 0.117 ag

title: Toward space-optimal approximate colored indexes at scale
abstract: Searching current petabase-scale sequence repositories requires indexes that combine compact storage with high query throughput. Although exact colored indexes retain complete sequence information, their construction and storage costs can become substantial for highly diverse collections. Indexes based on approximate membership query (AMQ) filters offer a compact alternative with fast construction and queries. Being hash-based, these indexes support different seeding schemes without structural changes, while sampling can reduce storage requirements, construction time and query time by an order of magnitude. Within the AMQ framework, querying many independent filters causes scattered memory accesses, reducing throughput. This motivates interleaved filters, which address this weakness by storing filter slots contiguously by position, enabling cache-friendly access and simultaneous membership queries. However, existing implementations face a trade-off between guaranteed construction and space-efficiency. Here, we introduce a new indexing framework based on interleaved ZOR filters, fingerprint-based structures with guaranteed construction that require only approximately 1% more space t

title: MintCNA: A Unified Framework for Integrative Copy Number Profiling with Single-Cell Multi-Omics Data
abstract: Chromosomal copy number alterations (CNAs) are key drivers of tumor evolution, disease progression and therapeutic resistance, and their identification is critical for delineating tumor clonal structure. However, accurately detecting CNAs from single-cell data remains challenging as most existing CNA callers still analyze a single omics layer and are susceptible to assay-specific noise. Recently, single-cell multi-omics techniques have enabled joint sequencing of multiple molecular layers (e.g., genomics and transcriptomics) simultaneously in the same cells, yet computational methods that fully exploit such complementary multi-omics data for CNA analysis remain limited. Here, we present MintCNA, a unified framework for CNA detection from paired single-cell multi-omics data. MintCNA integrates deep-learning based denoising with a missingness-adjusted multivariate change-point detection procedure to enhance CNA profiling across omics layers. In simulations, MintCNA outperformed existing single-cell CNA callers across all evaluated scenarios. title: Development and Validation of a Multiple Linear Regression QSAR Model for the Prediction of Acute Aquatic Toxicity (LC₅₀) of Herbicides
abstract: The quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) approach constitutes a powerful computational framework for establishing systematic and quantitative correlations between molecular structure and measurable biological or toxicological endpoints. By integrating the strategic selection of molecular descriptors, encoding critical topological, electronic, and physicochemical features, with rigorous chemometric workflows and multivariate statistical modeling, this methodology delivers high predictive accuracy, internal stability, and external generalizability. In the present study, a QSAR model based on Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) was developed and rigorously validated for the prediction of acute aquatic toxicity, expressed as LC50, of a structurally diverse series of herbicides. A curated dataset of 110 compounds, sourced from peer-reviewed literature, was employed for model construction and validation. Dataset partitioning into training and external test sets was performed using the Kennard-Stone algorithm, ensuring representative and uniform coverage of the chemical descriptor space. title: BioLiP3: a protein-ligand affinity database integrating curated data with LLM-enabled literature mining
abstract: Quantitative binding affinities and three-dimensional protein-ligand structures provide complementary information essential for structure-based drug discovery, yet these data remain largely disconnected across existing databases and the biomedical literature. We present BioLiP3, a major extension of BioLiP that expands quantitative affinity coverage 13-fold within its structure-centered framework for biologically relevant interactions. BioLiP3 contains 593 423 affinity records, of which 591 820 are linked to three-dimensional protein-ligand structures: 45 386 experimentally resolved PDB complexes, 528 732 BindingDB-derived records with computationally generated structures, and 17 702 structure-linked records derived from LLM-mined biomedical literature. For records lacking experimental complex structures, we generate structural models using available experimental or predicted receptor structures, binding-site identification, and molecular docking, with experimental and computational structures explicitly distinguished. OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. Existing ST simulators model normal tissue and do not represent tumor evolution, CNA-driven expression, or the spatial organization of malignant subclones. We present OncoSpot, a cancer-aware simulator of Visium-like spot-based ST data. OncoSpot combines a spatial evolutionary scaffold from DEMON, CNAs generated along the resulting clonal phylogeny with CNAsim, cancer-type-specific malignant transcriptional programs, and spatially clustered nonmalignant cell types, and aggregates cells into spots with known malignant fraction, subclone, and copy-number profiles. We demonstrate OncoSpot on high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, which represent three distinct modes of tumor evolution. Simulated subclones were spatially clustered and showed stronger phylogeny-space concordance than those generated by scCube under matched subclone populations. Benchmarking CopyKA

title: FoldAbS: Repurposing the Protein Folding Model as a Foundation Encoder for Antibody Screening
abstract: Therapeutic antibody screening requires prioritizing antibody candidates across specificity, affinity, and developability. Current pipelines typically silo these objectives and underuse structural information that governs antibody-antigen recognition. To address these inefficacies, we introduce FoldAbS, a unified supervised screening framework that reconceptualizes protein folding models as frozen foundation encoders, exploiting their internal representations to capture rich sequence, geometric, and interaction dynamics well beyond basic structure prediction. By coupling the folding model with lightweight, task-specific heads, FoldAbS seamlessly evaluates all three therapeutic criteria within a single architecture. Instantiating this framework with the open-source Protenix model (FoldAbS-Px) yields consistent improvements over baseline approaches, achieving significant performance gains of up to 13.1%, 9.2%, and 6.2% in specificity, affinity, and developability, respectively. Collectively, these results reposition protein folding models from structure predictors and confidence scorers into reusable foundation encoders for comprehensive and supervised antibody screening. title: Translating chemical reactions into enzyme sequences enables formate dehydrogenase engineering
abstract: Enzyme engineering has broad applications across chemistry and biotechnology but remains costly and susceptible to low success rates. Generative artificial intelligence can substantially expand the sequence space accessible to enzyme engineering; however, directing generation towards enzymes that catalyse a user-defined chemical reaction remains challenging. Inspired by machine translation, we formulate enzyme generation as translation between two molecular languages: chemical reactions and amino acid sequences. Here, we introduce REXzyme, a translation model that generates enzymes conditioned on user-defined reactions. First, we evaluate its designs using multiple in silico metrics and characterize the strengths and limitations of its generalisation capacity. Then, we steer REXzyme towards the generation of enhanced formate dehydrogenases for their reverse natural reaction, i.e., the reduction of carbon dioxide. All 20 generated enzymes were expressed and purified as soluble proteins and exhibited CO2-reduction activity, with the most active design reaching 2.5-fold the specific activity of the reference enzyme. title: Protify: A Benchmarking Platform Revealing Task Dependence and Homology Leakage in Protein Language Model Evaluation
abstract: Protein Language Models (pLMs) have become essential tools for computational protein analysis, and the rapid proliferation of architectures, training objectives, and pretraining corpora has produced a diverse and expanding model landscape. Evaluation practices, however, remain fragmented: studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and reporting conventions, so results rarely transfer between publications. Here we introduce Protify, an open-source platform that standardizes pLM benchmarking across zero-shot, supervised, and transferlearning settings through a unified, low-code interface. Protify currently supports 35 pretrained models and 61 curated datasets and it is easy to add custom versions of each. Leveraging Protify's high throughput pipelines, we benchmarked 23 models on ProteinGym, discovering that DPLM3B is currently the top-performing self-supervised encoder. Another large-scale supervised evaluation across 32 diverse tasks, spanning enzyme classification, gene ontology annotation, protein-protein interaction, subcellular localization, and other functional properties, found that no single pLM dominated: 14 different models took the top score on at least one

title: Towards Robust Automated Mouse Scratching Behavior Detection for Itch Research
abstract: Quantification of mouse scratching behavior is essential for preclinical itch research. However, manual video annotation is labor-intensive, and automated detection remains challenging in terms of accuracy and generalizability. We present Scratch-AID+, a computational framework dedicated to automated mouse scratching detection, including a diverse and progressive set of model families and learning strategies: classic ResNet-based detectors, task-adaptive fine-tuning of video foundation models, and in-context learning of advanced multimodal large language models. To simulate real-world use cases, we benchmark on a public dataset containing annotated video recordings from a source laboratory with additional cross-laboratory videos for independent testing, and we explore different data preprocessing and training configurations. We find that classic models suffer severe performance degradation on external data under our realistic setting with sparse scratching events. In contrast, fine-tuned video foundation models substantially improve the generalizability, achieving significantly better detection performance. Computational Analysis of Antioxidant Effects on Stress Response Mechanisms in Candida albicans
abstract: Candida albicans was used as a eukaryotic model to study aging and oxidative stress response pathways focused on NAD dependent deacetylases, Sir2 and SIRT3. A significant gene expression regulation of both Sir2 and SIRT3 was observed under sublethal hydrogen peroxide treatment towards their association with stress adaptation. Natural ligands known for antioxidant properties were docked against Sir2 and SIRT3 structures. Binding free energy of most components fall in the range of -5.0 to -11 kcal/mol. The best candidates pterostilbene, quercetin and naringenin formed stable hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds within catalytic and NAD binding pockets confirmed by visualization. Detailed ADME profiling shows most of the ligands passed the Lipinski rule of five and revealed a very good gastrointestinal absorption. PASS (Prediction of Activity Spectra for Substances) and SOM (Sites of Metabolism) predicts antioxidants, anti-aging properties, toxicity profiles, with key metabolic hotspots. This integrated in-silico approach highlights naringenin and quercetin as promising modulators of Sir2/SIRT3 mediated metabolic pathways in Candida albicans, warranting further validation with

title: Ark-ADMET: endpoint-specific selection of molecular representations and hyperparameters for gradient-boosted ADMET models under the Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark protocol
abstract: Typical submissions to the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) benchmark leaderboard apply a single architecture and a single feature representation across all 22 endpoints, despite substantial heterogeneity in evaluation metric, training-set size, and class balance. Rather than proposing a new architecture, we show that endpoint-specific selection of molecular representations and CatBoost hyperparameters, carried out under the official TDC ADMET benchmark protocol, is a competitive alternative to that uniform recipe. For each endpoint, a fixed CatBoost backbone was paired with configurations chosen from a common candidate set comprising published fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors, truncated three-dimensional PaDEL descriptors, frozen graph isomorphism network (GIN) and MiniMol embeddings, and a convex combination with a shallow network trained on the MiniMol embedding alone. All feature and hyperparameter choices were made on an internal scaffold validation split under a prespecified strict-improvement rule.
